question:
I want to study the robotics techniques described in the PDF “RT-2, Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control” located in my pdf/embodied_ai_papers folder.  
    Can you extract the main technical ideas from that PDF, look up the current best‑practice APIs or libraries that support similar vision‑language robotics workflows, and then save a concise summary of those findings into my long‑term memory as a new knowledge item?
answer:
Done. Here's what I found and saved.

## 1. RT-2's main technical ideas (from the PDF, pp. 1–10)

**The core claim:** a single end-to-end model can both map robot observations → actions *and* inherit web-scale vision-language knowledge, if you co-fine-tune a big VLM on robot trajectories.

- **"Actions as another language."** The 8-D action (6-DoF end-effector delta x/y/z + rotations, gripper extension, plus a discrete `terminate`) is discretized into 256 uniform bins and emitted as ordinary text tokens: `terminate Δpos_x Δpos_y Δpos_z Δrot_x Δrot_y Δrot_z gripper_ext`. No new heads, no action-only layers — weights are fully shared with language.
- **Tokenizer-specific action vocabulary:** PaLI-X has unique integer tokens up to 1000 (map directly); PaLM-E gets its 256 least-frequent tokens overwritten (symbol tuning).
- **Co-fine-tuning beats plain fine-tuning.** Mixing the original web VQA/captioning data with robot data prevents catastrophic forgetting — and training from scratch is very poor. Bigger models generalize better (55B > 5B).
- **Constrained decoding** restricts the vocabulary to valid action tokens only on robot prompts.
- **Serving pattern for real-time control:** the 55B model can't live on a robot GPU, so it's hosted as a cloud service queried over the network (1–3 Hz at 55B, ~5 Hz at 5B) — the direct ancestor of today's policy-server + thin-client design.
- **Results:** ~6,000 trials; ~2× over RT-1/MOO and ~6× over VC-1/R3M on unseen objects/backgrounds/environments; emergent capabilities (symbol understanding, arithmetic/multilingual reasoning, person recognition) >3× the best baseline; a chain-of-thought "Plan:" variant adds multi-stage reasoning.
- **Limitation:** motor skills stay bounded by the robot data — web knowledge re-purposes skills, it doesn't create new ones.

## 2. Current best-practice libraries for similar VLA workflows

- **LeRobot** (`/huggingface/lerobot`, v0.6.1) — the closest end-to-end match: `LeRobotDataset` + `record_loop` for teleop data collection, `lerobot-train --policy.type={pi0|smolvla|act|diffusion}` (SmolVLA's `--policy.load_vlm_weights=true` is the analogue of VLM-initialized policies), `lerobot-rollout` for deployment, **Real-Time Chunking** (`--inference.type=rtc`) to fix exactly the latency problem RT-2 hit, and an async client/server inference split.
- **OpenPI** (`/physical-intelligence/openpi`) — open pi0/pi0.5 checkpoints plus `scripts/serve_policy.py` (port 8000) and `WebsocketClientPolicy` returning action chunks; essentially RT-2's cloud-inference idea turned into a supported API.

## 3. Saved to long-term memory

A new knowledge item **"RT-2 VLA Models - Technical Summary"** (12 observations covering the architecture, action tokenization, training recipe, ablations, serving pattern, results, and limitations), plus two linked library entities — **LeRobot** and **OpenPI** — connected via relations *"is implemented in practice with"* and *"has serving pattern continued by"*.

content.text:
### Run rollout with Real-Time Chunking (--inference.type=rtc)

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/inference.mdx

Run a rollout with the Real-Time Chunking (RTC) inference backend. Use this for large, slow VLA models like Pi0, Pi0.5, or SmolVLA to achieve smooth, continuous motion despite high inference latency. The example sets an execution horizon of 10 and a max guidance weight of 10.0; other RTC flags (mode, prefix_attention_schedule, queue_threshold) are available and documented in the table.

```bash
lerobot-rollout \
    --strategy.type=base \
    --inference.type=rtc \
    --inference.rtc.execution_horizon=10 \
    --inference.rtc.max_guidance_weight=10.0 \
    --policy.path=${HF_USER}/pi0_policy \
    --robot.type=so100_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
    --robot.cameras="{ front: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 0, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30}}" \
    --task="Pick up the cube" \
    --duration=60 \
    --device=cuda
```

--------------------------------

### Run inference with lerobot-rollout

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/cheat-sheet.mdx

Run inference with the trained policy on a robot using lerobot-rollout. Provide the policy path (local or Hugging Face), robot type, port, camera configuration, task description, and duration in seconds. If duration is unspecified, it runs forever. Cameras must match the dataset collection configuration.

```bash
lerobot-rollout \
    --strategy.type=base \
    --policy.path=${HF_USER}/my_policy \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM1 \
    --robot.cameras="{ up: {type: opencv, index_or_path: /dev/video1, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30}, side: {type: opencv, index_or_path: /dev/video5, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30}}" \
    --task="Put lego brick into the transparent box" \
    --duration=60
```

--------------------------------

### Run real-time inference with lerobot-rollout

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/smolvla.mdx

Run inference with the finetuned model on a SO-101 follower arm. Requires being logged in to the HuggingFace Hub. Replace the port, robot id, camera configuration, task description, and policy path with your own values. Optional RTC and teleop flags are commented out.

```bash
lerobot-rollout \
  --strategy.type=base \
  --robot.type=so101_follower \
  --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \ # <- Use your port
  --robot.id=my_blue_follower_arm \ # <- Use your robot id
  --robot.cameras="{ front: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 8, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30}}" \ # <- Use your cameras
  --task="Grasp a lego block and put it in the bin." \ # <- Use the same task description you used in your dataset recording
  # <- RTC optional, use when running on low power hardware \
  # --inference.type=rtc \
  # --inference.rtc.execution_horizon=10 \
  # --inference.rtc.max_guidance_weight=10.0 \
  # <- Teleop optional if you want to teleoperate in between episodes \
  # --teleop.type=so100_leader \
  # --teleop.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
  # --teleop.id=my_red_leader_arm \
  # --display_data=true #optional use if you want to see the camera stream \
  --policy.path=HF_USER/FINETUNE_MODEL_NAME # <- Use your fine-tuned model
```

### Train SmolVLA on LIBERO-plus

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/libero_plus.mdx

Train a SmolVLA policy on the LIBERO-plus dataset. Requires the lerobot/libero_plus dataset and sets --env.type=libero_plus with the task libero_spatial. Uses 100000 steps, batch size 4, and evaluates every 1000 steps.

```bash
lerobot-train \
    --policy.type=smolvla \
    --policy.repo_id=${HF_USER}/smolvla_libero_plus \
    --policy.load_vlm_weights=true \
    --dataset.repo_id=lerobot/libero_plus \
    --env.type=libero_plus \
    --env.task=libero_spatial \
    --output_dir=./outputs/ \
    --steps=100000 \
    --batch_size=4 \
    --eval.batch_size=1 \
    --eval.n_episodes=1 \
    --env_eval_freq=1000
```

--------------------------------

### Launch the Robot Client with RobotClientConfig

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/async.mdx

Complete setup for launching the RobotClient in the async inference pipeline. It creates the follower robot with two OpenCV cameras, configures the client with server address, policy device, and pretrained model, then starts the client, runs the control loop, and handles KeyboardInterrupt by stopping and optionally plotting the action queue size.

```python
import threading
from lerobot.robots.so_follower import SO100FollowerConfig
from lerobot.cameras.opencv import OpenCVCameraConfig
from lerobot.async_inference.configs import RobotClientConfig
from lerobot.async_inference.robot_client import RobotClient
from lerobot.async_inference.helpers import visualize_action_queue_size

# 1. Create the robot instance
"""Check out the cameras available in your setup by running `python lerobot/find_cameras.py`"""
# these cameras must match the ones expected by the policy
# check the config.json on the Hub for the policy you are using
camera_cfg = {
    "top": OpenCVCameraConfig(index_or_path=0, width=640, height=480, fps=30),
    "side": OpenCVCameraConfig(index_or_path=1, width=640, height=480, fps=30)
}

robot_cfg = SO100FollowerConfig(
  port="/dev/tty.usbmodem585A0076841",
  id="follower_so100",
  cameras=camera_cfg
)

# 3. Create client configuration
client_cfg = RobotClientConfig(
    robot=robot_cfg,
    server_address="localhost:8080",
    policy_device="mps",
    client_device="cpu",
    policy_type="smolvla",
    pretrained_name_or_path="<user>/smolvla_async",
    chunk_size_threshold=0.5,
    actions_per_chunk=50,  # make sure this is less than the max actions of the policy
)

# 4. Create and start client
client = RobotClient(client_cfg)

# 5. Specify the task
task = "Don't do anything, stay still"

if client.start():
    # Start action receiver thread
    action_receiver_thread = threading.Thread(target=client.receive_actions, daemon=True)
    action_receiver_thread.start()

    try:
        # Run the control loop
        client.control_loop(task)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        client.stop()
        action_receiver_thread.join()
        # (Optionally) plot the action queue size
        visualize_action_queue_size(client.action_queue_size)
```

content.text:
### Query remote policy server with WebsocketClientPolicy

Source: https://github.com/physical-intelligence/openpi/blob/main/docs/remote_inference.md

Queries the remote policy server from robot code. Initializes the client, constructs an observation dictionary with resized uint8 images and unnormalized state, and calls infer to get an action chunk. The host and port default to localhost:8000.

```python
from openpi_client import image_tools
from openpi_client import websocket_client_policy

# Outside of episode loop, initialize the policy client.
# Point to the host and port of the policy server (localhost and 8000 are the defaults).
client = websocket_client_policy.WebsocketClientPolicy(host="localhost", port=8000)

for step in range(num_steps):
    # Inside the episode loop, construct the observation.
    # Resize images on the client side to minimize bandwidth / latency. Always return images in uint8 format.
    # We provide utilities for resizing images + uint8 conversion so you match the training routines.
    # The typical resize_size for pre-trained pi0 models is 224.
    # Note that the proprioceptive `state` can be passed unnormalized, normalization will be handled on the server side.
    observation = {
        "observation/image": image_tools.convert_to_uint8(
            image_tools.resize_with_pad(img, 224, 224)
        ),
        "observation/wrist_image": image_tools.convert_to_uint8(
            image_tools.resize_with_pad(wrist_img, 224, 224)
        ),
        "observation/state": state,
        "prompt": task_instruction,
    }

    # Call the policy server with the current observation.
    # This returns an action chunk of shape (action_horizon, action_dim).
    # Note that you typically only need to call the policy every N steps and execute steps
    # from the predicted action chunk open-loop in the remaining steps.
    action_chunk = client.infer(observation)["actions"]

    # Execute the actions in the environment.
    ...
```

--------------------------------

### Serve policy server for inference

Source: https://github.com/physical-intelligence/openpi/blob/main/README.md

Launches a policy server that listens on port 8000 and waits for observations. Uses the checkpoint for iteration 20,000; modify as needed.

```bash
uv run scripts/serve_policy.py policy:checkpoint --policy.config=pi05_libero --policy.dir=checkpoints/pi05_libero/my_experiment/20000
```

--------------------------------

### Running openpi models remotely > Starting a remote policy server

Source: https://github.com/physical-intelligence/openpi/blob/main/docs/remote_inference.md

To start a remote policy server, you can simply run the following command:

```bash
uv run scripts/serve_policy.py --env=[DROID | ALOHA | LIBERO]
```

The `env` argument specifies which $\pi_0$ checkpoint should be loaded. Under the hood, this script will execute a command like the following, which you can use to start a policy server, e.g. for checkpoints you trained yourself (here an example for the DROID environment):

```bash
uv run scripts/serve_policy.py policy:checkpoint --policy.config=pi0_fast_droid --policy.dir=gs://openpi-assets/checkpoints/pi0_fast_droid
```

This will start a policy server that will serve the policy specified by the `config` and `dir` arguments. The policy will be served on the specified port (default: 8000).

--------------------------------

### serve_policy.py

Source: https://github.com/physical-intelligence/openpi/blob/main/README.md

Script to launch a policy server for inference.

```APIDOC
## [SCRIPT] serve_policy.py

### Description
Spins up a policy server that listens on port 8000 and waits for observations to be sent to it.

### Usage
```bash
uv run scripts/serve_policy.py policy:checkpoint --policy.config=pi05_libero --policy.dir=checkpoints/pi05_libero/my_experiment/20000
```

### Parameters
#### Command Line Arguments
- **policy:checkpoint** (string) - Required - Specifies the checkpoint to load.
- **--policy.config** (string) - Required - Name of the policy config (e.g., `pi05_libero`).
- **--policy.dir** (string) - Required - Path to the checkpoint directory.

```

--------------------------------

### Running openpi models remotely > Querying the remote policy server from your robot code

Source: https://github.com/physical-intelligence/openpi/blob/main/docs/remote_inference.md

We provide a client utility with minimal dependencies that you can easily embed into any robot codebase.

First, install the `openpi-client` package in your robot environment:

```bash
cd $OPENPI_ROOT/packages/openpi-client
pip install -e .
```

Then, you can use the client to query the remote policy server from your robot code. Here's an example of how to do this:

```python
from openpi_client import image_tools
from openpi_client import websocket_client_policy

# Outside of episode loop, initialize the policy client.
# Point to the host and port of the policy server (localhost and 8000 are the defaults).
client = websocket_client_policy.WebsocketClientPolicy(host="localhost", port=8000)

for step in range(num_steps):
    # Inside the episode loop, construct the observation.
    # Resize images on the client side to minimize bandwidth / latency. Always return images in uint8 format.
    # We provide utilities for resizing images + uint8 conversion so you match the training routines.
    # The typical resize_size for pre-trained pi0 models is 224.
    # Note that the proprioceptive `state` can be passed unnormalized, normalization will be handled on the server side.
    observation = {
        "observation/image": image_tools.convert_to_uint8(
            image_tools.resize_with_pad(img, 224, 224)
        ),
        "observation/wrist_image": image_tools.convert_to_uint8(
            image_tools.resize_with_pad(wrist_img, 224, 224)
        ),
        "observation/state": state,
        "prompt": task_instruction,
    }

    # Call the policy server with the current observation.
    # This returns an action chunk of shape (action_horizon, action_dim).
    # Note that you typically only need to call the policy every N steps and execute steps
    # from the predicted action chunk open-loop in the remaining steps.
    action_chunk = client.infer(observation)["actions"]

    # Execute the actions in the environment.
    ...

```

Here, the `host` and `port` arguments specify the IP address and port of the remote policy server. You can also specify these as command-line arguments to your robot code, or hard-code them in your robot codebase. The `observation` is a dictionary of observations and the prompt, following the specification of the policy inputs for the policy you are serving. We have concrete examples of how to construct this dictionary for different environments in the [simple client example](../examples/simple_client/main.py).

### Specify Pi0 policy type

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/pi0.mdx

Set the policy type to 'pi0' in your LeRobot configuration to use the Pi0 policy.

```python
policy.type=pi0
```

--------------------------------

### Record a dataset with SO-101 arms using LeRobotDataset and record_loop

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/il_robots.mdx

Complete script to record a dataset with the SO-101 follower and leader arms. It configures cameras, creates a LeRobotDataset, runs record_loop for each episode, handles re-recording and resets, then finalizes and pushes the dataset to the Hub. Requires the robot and teleoperator ports and a valid Hugging Face repo ID.

```python
from lerobot.cameras.opencv import OpenCVCameraConfig
from lerobot.datasets.lerobot_dataset import LeRobotDataset
from lerobot.utils.feature_utils import hw_to_dataset_features
from lerobot.robots.so_follower import SO101Follower, SO101FollowerConfig
from lerobot.teleoperators.so_leader.config_so_leader import SO101LeaderConfig
from lerobot.teleoperators.so_leader.so_leader import SO101Leader
from lerobot.common.control_utils import init_keyboard_listener
from lerobot.utils.utils import log_say
from lerobot.utils.visualization_utils import init_visualization
from lerobot.scripts.lerobot_record import record_loop
from lerobot.processor import make_default_processors

NUM_EPISODES = 5
FPS = 30
EPISODE_TIME_SEC = 60
RESET_TIME_SEC = 10
TASK_DESCRIPTION = "My task description"

def main():
    # Create robot configuration
    robot_config = SO101FollowerConfig(
        port="/dev/tty.usbmodem5AB90687491",
        id="my_follower_arm",
        cameras={
            "wrist": OpenCVCameraConfig(index_or_path=0, width=640, height=480, fps=30),
            "top": OpenCVCameraConfig(index_or_path=1, width=640, height=480, fps=30)
        }
    )

    teleop_config = SO101LeaderConfig(
        port="/dev/tty.usbmodem5AB90689011",
        id="my_leader_arm",
    )

    # Initialize the robot and teleoperator
    robot = SO101Follower(robot_config)
    teleop = SO101Leader(teleop_config)

    # Configure the dataset features
    action_features = hw_to_dataset_features(robot.action_features, "action")
    obs_features = hw_to_dataset_features(robot.observation_features, "observation")
    dataset_features = {**action_features, **obs_features}

    # Create the dataset
    dataset = LeRobotDataset.create(
        repo_id="<hf_username>/<dataset_repo_id>",
        fps=FPS,
        features=dataset_features,
        robot_type=robot.name,
        use_videos=True,
        image_writer_threads=4,
    )

    # Initialize the keyboard listener and rerun visualization
    _, events = init_keyboard_listener()
    init_visualization("rerun", session_name="recording")

    # Connect the robot and teleoperator
    robot.connect()
    teleop.connect()

    # Create the required processors
    teleop_action_processor, robot_action_processor, robot_observation_processor = make_default_processors()

    episode_idx = 0
    while episode_idx < NUM_EPISODES and not events["stop_recording"]:
        log_say(f"Recording episode {episode_idx + 1} of {NUM_EPISODES}")

        record_loop(
            robot=robot,
            events=events,
            fps=FPS,
            teleop_action_processor=teleop_action_processor,
            robot_action_processor=robot_action_processor,
            robot_observation_processor=robot_observation_processor,
            teleop=teleop,
            dataset=dataset,
            control_time_s=EPISODE_TIME_SEC,
            single_task=TASK_DESCRIPTION,
            display_data=True,
        )

        # Reset the environment if not stopping or re-recording
        if not events["stop_recording"] and (episode_idx < NUM_EPISODES - 1 or events["rerecord_episode"]):
            log_say("Reset the environment")
            record_loop(
                robot=robot,
                events=events,
                fps=FPS,
                teleop_action_processor=teleop_action_processor,
                robot_action_processor=robot_action_processor,
                robot_observation_processor=robot_observation_processor,
                teleop=teleop,
                control_time_s=RESET_TIME_SEC,
                single_task=TASK_DESCRIPTION,
                display_data=True,
            )

        if events["rerecord_episode"]:
            log_say("Re-recording episode")
            events["rerecord_episode"] = False
            events["exit_early"] = False
            dataset.clear_episode_buffer()
            continue

        dataset.save_episode()
        episode_idx += 1

    # finalize dataset
    log_say("Finalizing dataset...")
    dataset.finalize()
    # Clean up
    log_say("Stop recording")
    robot.disconnect()
    teleop.disconnect()
    dataset.push_to_hub()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

--------------------------------

### Train Pi0 with LeRobot

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/pi0.mdx

Use this command to train a Pi0 model with the standard LeRobot training script. It includes configuration for dataset, policy type, output directory, and various training parameters.

```bash
lerobot-train \
    --dataset.repo_id=your_dataset \
    --policy.type=pi0 \
    --output_dir=./outputs/pi0_training \
    --job_name=pi0_training \
    --policy.pretrained_path=lerobot/pi0_base \
    --policy.repo_id=your_repo_id \
    --policy.compile_model=true \
    --policy.gradient_checkpointing=true \
    --policy.dtype=bfloat16 \
    --policy.freeze_vision_encoder=false \
    --policy.train_expert_only=false \
    --steps=3000 \
    --policy.device=cuda \
    --batch_size=32
```

--------------------------------

### Record dataset during OpenArm teleoperation

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/docs/source/openarm.mdx

Record a dataset during teleoperation. Uses lerobot-record with openarm_follower and openarm_leader types, specifying the Hugging Face repo ID, frames per second (fps=30), and number of episodes (num-episodes=10).

```bash
lerobot-record \
    --robot.type=openarm_follower \
    --robot.port=can0 \
    --robot.side=right \
    --robot.id=my_follower \
    --teleop.type=openarm_leader \
    --teleop.port=can1 \
    --teleop.id=my_leader \
    --repo-id=my_hf_username/my_openarm_dataset \
    --fps=30 \
    --num-episodes=10
```

--------------------------------

### Train ACT policy with lerobot-train

Source: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/examples/omx/README.md

Train an ACT policy on the collected dataset using the lerobot-train CLI. Requires the dataset repo ID and outputs to the specified directory. Enables Weights & Biases logging.

```bash
lerobot-train \
    --dataset.repo_id=$HF_USERNAME/omx_pickandplace \
    --policy.type=act \
    --output_dir=outputs/train/omx_pickandplace_act \
    --policy.device=cuda \
    --policy.repo_id=$HF_USERNAME/omx_pickandplace_act \
    --steps=20000 \
    --wandb.enable=true
```

No new action-specific parameters or heads are added - weights stay fully shared between language and action tasks.\", \"Token binding depends on tokenizer: PaLI-X has unique tokens for integers up to 1000 (map bins directly to integer tokens); PaLM-E lacks this, so the 256 least-frequently-used tokens are overwritten as action tokens (a form of symbol tuning).\", \"Training data format: VQA-style 'Q: what action should the robot take to [instruction]? A: <action tokens>'; robot data (RT-1 dataset, 13 robots, 17 months, office kitchen) is mixed with web VQA/captioning data.\", \"Key ablation result: co-fine-tuning (robot + original web data) beats (a) training from scratch (very poor) and (b) fine-tuning on robot data only; mixing prevents catastrophic forgetting of VLM concepts. Larger models generalize better (55B > 5B).\", \"Constrained decoding: when prompted with a robot-action task, restrict the output vocabulary to valid action tokens; on standard VQA tasks allow the full natural-language vocabulary.\", \"Deployment/serving pattern for real-time control: at 55B, on-robot GPUs are infeasible, so the model is served as a multi-TPU cloud service queried over the network by many robots (1-3 Hz at 55B, ~5 Hz at 5B; 3B PaLI sim variant ~5 Hz). This is the ancestor of today's 'policy server + thin robot client' architecture.\", \"Evaluation: ~6,000 real-world trials on a 7-DoF mobile manipulator. Seen-task success comparable to RT-1; on unseen objects/backgrounds/environments RT-2 gives ~2x over RT-1 and MOO, ~6x over VC-1/R3M baselines. Language-Table sim: RT-2-PaLI-3B 90±10 vs LAVA 77±4, RT-1 74±13, BC-Zero 72±3.\", \"Emergent capabilities from web pretraining (never in robot data): symbol understanding ('move apple to 3', 'push coke can on top of heart'), reasoning (same-color matching, arithmetic 'move X near the sum of two plus one', multilingual commands), and human recognition ('move the coke can to the person with glasses'). Best RT-2-PaLI-X is >3x the next best baseline (RT-1) on these.\", \"Chain-of-thought variant: a few hundred gradient steps on augmented data with an explicit 'Plan:' sentence before action tokens, e.g. 'Instruction: I'm hungry. Plan: pick rxbar chocolate. Action: 1 128 124 136 121 158 111 255.' Bridges VQA data and manipulation data, and unifies high-level planning with low-level control in one model (e.g. pick a rock as an improvised hammer, an energy drink for a tired person).\", \"Stated limitation: the model's physical skills remain bounded by the robot data distribution; web knowledge only re-purposes existing skills semantically/visually, it does not create new motor skills.\"]}, {\"name\": \"LeRobot (HuggingFace) — VLA workflow APIs\", \"entityType\": \"software_library\", \"observations\": [\"Context7 ID /huggingface/lerobot; v0.6.1; high source reputation, ~4543 code snippets. This is the practical analogue of RT-2's teleop-collected demonstration pipeline.\", \"Training CLI: `lerobot-train --dataset.repo_id=... --policy.type={pi0|smolvla|act|diffusion} --policy.pretrained_path=lerobot/pi0_base --policy.compile_model=true --policy.gradient_checkpointing=true --policy.dtype=bfloat16 --batch_size=32 --steps=...`; `--policy.load_vlm_weights=true` for SmolVLA (VLM-initialized policy, closest analogue to RT-2 co-fine-tuning).\", \"Deployment CLI: `lerobot-rollout --policy.path=$HF_USER/my_policy --robot.type=so101_follower --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 --robot.cameras=\\\"{front: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 8, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30}}\\\" --task=\\\"...\\\" --duration=60`.\", \"Handles RT-2's inference-latency problem with Real-Time Chunking: `--inference.type=rtc --inference.rtc.execution_horizon=10 --inference.rtc.max_guidance_weight=10.0` (plus mode, prefix_attention_schedule, queue_threshold) for smooth motion with large slow VLAs.\", \"Also ships an async inference client/server split mirroring RT-2's cloud policy service: RobotClientConfig(robot=..., server_address='localhost:8080', policy_type='smolvla', pretrained_name_or_path=..., actions_per_chunk=50); client.control_loop(task) with a separate receive_actions thread and visualize_action_queue_size().\"]}, {\"name\": \"OpenPI (Physical Intelligence) — VLA serving APIs\", \"entityType\": \"software_library\", \"observations\": [\"Context7 ID /physical-intelligence/openpi; high source reputation, ~203 snippets. Open checkpoints and packages for flow-matching VLA models (pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5) with fine-tuning examples for DROID/ALOHA/LIBERO.\", \"Policy server: `uv run scripts/serve_policy.py policy:checkpoint --policy.config=pi05_libero --policy.dir=checkpoints/.../20000` (or `--env=[DROID|ALOHA|LIBERO]`); listens on port 8000 for observations. Direct descendant of RT-2's out-of-process multi-TPU policy service.\", \"Thin client: `WebsocketClientPolicy(host='localhost', port=8000)`; observation dict keys 'observation/image', 'observation/wrist_image' (uint8, resize_with_pad to 224), 'observation/state' (unnormalized; server normalizes), 'prompt'; `client.infer(obs)['actions']` returns an action chunk of shape (action_horizon, action_dim) - call the policy every N steps and execute the chunk open-loop. Install via `pip install -e packages/openpi-client`.\"}]}]"}

entities.name: RT-2 VLA Models - Technical Summary
observations: Source: PDF 'RT-2, Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control' (Brohan et al., Google DeepMind, 2023, arXiv:2307.15818v1, 26 pages; site robotics-transformer2.github.io). Summary from pp.1-10.

Core idea: co-fine-tune a large pretrained vision-language model (PaLI-X 5B/55B, PaLM-E 12B) directly on robot trajectories so a single end-to-end model maps camera observations + text instructions to low-level actions while retaining Internet-scale vision-language knowledge.

Central trick ('actions as another language'): discretize the 8-D action vector (6-DoF end-effector delta position/rotation, gripper extension, plus a discrete terminate command) into 256 uniform bins per continuous dim, emitted as ordinary text tokens in the string 'terminate dpos_x dpos_y dpos_z drot_x drot_y drot_z gripper_extension'. No new action-specific parameters or heads - weights fully shared between language and action tasks.

Token binding depends on tokenizer: PaLI-X has unique integer tokens up to 1000 (map bins directly); PaLM-E lacks this, so the 256 least-frequently-used tokens are overwritten as action tokens (a form of symbol tuning).

Training format: VQA-style 'Q: what action should the robot take to [instruction]? A: <action tokens>'; robot data (RT-1 dataset, 13 robots, 17 months, office kitchen) mixed with web VQA/captioning data.

Key ablation: co-fine-tuning (robot + original web data) beats training from scratch (very poor) and robot-data-only fine-tuning; mixing prevents catastrophic forgetting. Larger models generalize better (55B > 5B).
Constrained decoding: for robot-action prompts restrict the output vocabulary to valid action tokens; on standard VQA tasks allow the full natural-language vocabulary.

Real-time serving pattern: at 55B on-robot GPUs are infeasible, so the model is served as a multi-TPU cloud service queried over the network by many robots (1-3 Hz at 55B, ~5 Hz at 5B; 3B PaLI sim variant ~5 Hz). Ancestor of today's policy-server + thin robot-client architecture.

Evaluation: ~6,000 real-world trials on a 7-DoF mobile manipulator. Seen-task success comparable to RT-1; on unseen objects/backgrounds/environments ~2x over RT-1 and MOO, ~6x over VC-1/R3M. Language-Table sim: RT-2-PaLI-3B 90+/-10 vs LAVA 77+/-4, RT-1 74+/-13, BC-Zero 72+/-3.

Emergent capabilities from web pretraining (never in robot data): symbol understanding ('move apple to 3', 'push coke can on top of heart'), reasoning (same-color matching, arithmetic, multilingual commands), human recognition ('move the coke can to the person with glasses'). Best RT-2-PaLI-X is >3x the next best baseline (RT-1) on these.

Chain-of-thought variant: a few hundred gradient steps on data augmented with an explicit 'Plan:' sentence before action tokens, e.g. 'Instruction: I am hungry. Plan: pick rxbar chocolate. Action: 1 128 124 136 121 158 111 255.' Bridges VQA data and manipulation data; unifies high-level planning with low-level control in one model.
Stated limitation: physical skills remain bounded by the robot data distribution; web knowledge re-purposes existing skills semantically/visually, it does not create new motor skills.

entities.name: LeRobot (HuggingFace) - VLA workflow APIs
observations: Context7 ID /huggingface/lerobot; v0.6.1; high reputation, ~4543 snippets. End-to-end learning for real robots (SO-100/SO-101, OpenArm).

Data collection: LeRobotDataset.create(repo_id, fps, features, robot_type, use_videos=True, image_writer_threads=4) + record_loop(...) with teleop leader arm (SO101Leader), make_default_processors(), save_episode()/finalize()/push_to_hub().

Training CLI: lerobot-train --dataset.repo_id=... --policy.type={pi0|smolvla|act|diffusion} --policy.pretrained_path=lerobot/pi0_base --policy.compile_model=true --policy.gradient_checkpointing=true --policy.dtype=bfloat16 --batch_size=32; --policy.load_vlm_weights=true for SmolVLA (VLM-initialized policy, closest analogue to RT-2 co-fine-tuning).

Deployment CLI: lerobot-rollout --policy.path=$HF_USER/my_policy --robot.type=so101_follower --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 --robot.cameras="{front: {type: opencv, index_or_path: 8, width: 640, height: 480, fps: 30}}" --task="..." --duration=60.

Handles RT-2's inference-latency problem via Real-Time Chunking: --inference.type=rtc --inference.rtc.execution_horizon=10 --inference.rtc.max_guidance_weight=10.0 (plus mode, prefix_attention_schedule, queue_threshold).

Async inference client/server split mirrors RT-2's cloud policy service: RobotClientConfig(server_address='localhost:8080', policy_type='smolvla', actions_per_chunk=50); client.control_loop(task) with a receive_actions thread and visualize_action_queue_size().

entities.name: OpenPI (Physical Intelligence) - VLA serving APIs
observations: Context7 ID /physical-intelligence/openpi; high reputation, ~203 snippets. Open checkpoints and packages for flow-matching VLA models (pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5) with fine-tuning examples for DROID/ALOHA/LIBERO.

Policy server: uv run scripts/serve_policy.py policy:checkpoint --policy.config=pi05_libero --policy.dir=checkpoints/.../20000 (or --env=[DROID|ALOHA|LIBERO]); listens on port 8000. Direct descendant of RT-2's out-of-process policy service.

Thin client: WebsocketClientPolicy(host='localhost', port=8000); observation dict keys 'observation/image', 'observation/wrist_image' (uint8, resize_with_pad to 224), 'observation/state' (unnormalized, server normalizes), 'prompt'; client.infer(obs)['actions'] returns an action chunk (action_horizon, action_dim) - call every N steps and execute open-loop. Install via pip install -e packages/openpi-client.
